overview: The Bangwato state was an influential Tswana polity in what is now Botswana. Under Khama III, diplomacy helped defend it against takeover by Cecil Rhodes’s company, while British protectorate rule constrained its independence. This map shows only part of a longer history of changing capitals and continuing communities.

periods.title: The Shoshong years
periods.summary: Shoshong remained the capital until Khama’s move to Phalatswe in 1889.

periods.title: Phalatswe, or Old Palapye
periods.summary: A large new capital faced pressure on water and grazing, drought and cattle disease.

periods.title: Serowe and continuing rule
periods.summary: The capital moved to Serowe in 1902; the map endpoint is not the end of Bangwato society.

sections.title: Diplomacy, authority and a moving capital

items.text: In 1895, Khama III travelled to Britain with Sebele I and Bathoen I to oppose Rhodes’s expansion. Meetings and public campaigning helped keep their territories out of his company’s hands. The achievement preserved room for local rule, although the British protectorate remained a colonial arrangement.

Khama linked political authority closely to his Christian church. His correspondence shows that religious affiliation could affect permission to settle in his territory, and temperance rules were enforced through both church and chiefly power. His resistance to outside domination coexisted with restrictions on his own subjects.

Water helped decide where the capital stood. In 1900, a traveller reported women drawing water from deep wells in the Lotsane riverbed and paying grain for each pot. The move to Serowe in 1902 followed years of shortages, negotiations and population movements.

Drought and failed harvests were followed by rinderpest in 1896, killing most cattle. That was a household disaster as well as an economic one: livestock, crops and available water all came under pressure together.

Daily work linked the homestead, arable fields and cattle post. Women generally maintained homes and did much farming, while men and boys worked with cattle. Photographs taken around 1895 at Palapye show women thatching roofs and pounding maize: a busy household required far more than a roof overhead.

Three surviving tools make those activities tangible: a food-storage basket, an iron hoe for cultivation and weeding, and a multipurpose knife used at cattle posts. Museum researchers connect them to different working places rather than treating them as anonymous ornaments.

A wooden spoon collected in the 1890s is almost a metre long. It served communal cooking in large pots. This was serious stirring equipment: slipping it into a lunchbox would have been an ambitious plan.

One pair of 1890s sandals was made from the soft forehead skin of a cow. The collection also records clothing made from both leather and woven fabric. Skilled leatherworkers adapted familiar materials while tastes and available goods changed.

sections.title: Learning, women’s leadership and written words

items.text: Church schools opened new opportunities, but education remained unequal. Museum researchers note that girls often attended while boys worked at cattle posts, yet lessons channelled girls toward domestic subjects. School could widen a child’s possibilities and reinforce expectations about their future work at the same time.

Semane Setlhoko Khama was a teacher before becoming Khama’s wife in 1900. She supported women teachers and girls’ schooling, and later, under Tshekedi’s regency, promoted midwifery and medicine. Her work places education and children’s health alongside diplomacy in the story of political leadership.

“a re tshwarisane” means “let us work hard hand in hand” in the published translation of Khama’s Setswana letter dated 12 February 1923. He was discussing support for teachers. This attested phrase comes from correspondence after the map’s endpoint, showing that local writing and government continued.

In 2026, artefacts taken overseas during Khama’s reign returned to the Khama III Memorial Museum in Serowe. Their unveiling brought household objects, clothing and community memories back together. History here is also something living communities preserve and interpret for themselves.

ending.text: The imported record ends in 1914, but Khama III lived and ruled until 1923. The Bangwato community, its leadership and its cultural institutions continued through later political changes. The museum in Serowe now preserves objects and memories from this longer history.
